title: Le Chatelier's Principle
short: A system at equilibrium shifts to partly undo a change in concentration, pressure or temperature.
trouble: Students think adding a catalyst shifts an equilibrium, or that the shift undoes the change completely.

blocks.html: A system at Dynamic Equilibrium holds steady until something disturbs it. Then it shifts to a new balance. Predicting the direction uses the rates you know, plus Boyle's Law for what squeezing a gas does.

Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure (by changing the volume) or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the change. A catalyst causes no shift.

head: Change to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ)
Shift
Why
rows: uses up some of what was added
replaces some of what was removed
4 gas molecules become 2, lowering the pressure
blocks.cap: Predicting shifts for the synthesis of ammonia.

blocks.html: Adding a reactant makes forward collisions more frequent, so the forward rate jumps ahead until the extra reactant is partly used and the rates match again. Squeezing a gas mixture raises the pressure; the side with fewer gas molecules makes fewer collisions with the walls, so shifting toward it lowers the pressure. For temperature, treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction: adding heat pushes the reaction back. (Temperature is the one change that also changes the equilibrium constant, as you will see later.)

blocks.name: ch-equilibrium
blocks.cap: Extra nitrogen is added at time 20. The forward rate jumps, ammonia rises and hydrogen falls, and a new equilibrium forms. Nitrogen ends lower than right after the addition but higher than before it.

blocks.title: Adding a reactant
blocks.q: More $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ is added to $$\mathrm{N}_{2} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_{3}$$ at equilibrium. Which way does it shift?
steps: The added $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ speeds up the forward reaction.
The system shifts toward the products, using up part of the added nitrogen and making more ammonia.

blocks.title: Raising the pressure
blocks.q: The volume of $$\mathrm{N}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{4} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}_{2}$$ at equilibrium is cut in half. Which way does it shift?
steps: Count gas molecules: 1 on the left, 2 on the right.
Higher pressure favors the side with fewer gas molecules: the left.

blocks.title: Heating an exothermic reaction
blocks.q: The ammonia equilibrium above ($\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ}$) is heated. Which way does it shift?
steps: Forward is exothermic, so heat acts like a product.
Adding a product shifts the system toward the reactants.
blocks.a: Toward the reactants: less ammonia at equilibrium.

blocks.html: Thinking a catalyst shifts an equilibrium, or that the shift undoes a change completely. A catalyst only gets the system to equilibrium sooner. And after nitrogen is added, the new equilibrium still has more nitrogen than before; the shift only takes back part of the change.

The ammonia industry balances these effects. High pressure (roughly 150 to 300 atm) favors ammonia; low temperature favors it too but makes the reaction too slow, so plants run at about 400 to 500 °C with an iron catalyst.
